# Pañcakanipāta (AN 5)
**ID:** AN 5
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Pañcakanipāta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/an5

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pañcakanipāta* is the fifth major division of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, comprising discourses that organize the Buddha's teachings into numerical groups of five [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1994]. In the Pali Text Society arrangement, it constitutes Volume III of the collection and is divided into 26 chapters (*vagga*) [Hazra 1994]. SuttaCentral catalogs 91 distinct suttas with parallels in this branch [SuttaCentral]. The collection includes the *Muṇḍarājavagga*, which features King Muṇḍa being consoled upon his queen's death by the elder Nārada; because Muṇḍa ruled in Rājagaha several decades after the Buddha's *parinibbāna*, this section provides evidence for the ongoing compilation and chronological layering of the nikāya beyond the initial decades following the Buddha's demise [Hazra 1994].
Specific discourses in the *Pañcakanipāta* address various aspects of monastic discipline, meditation, doctrinal analysis, and practical care. For instance, AN 5.28 and AN 5.29 explore contemplative practices, detailing fivefold right concentration and the five practical benefits of walking meditation (*caṅkama*) [Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. AN 5.79 addresses future dangers to the monastic life and mentions doctrinal discussions (*abhidhammakathā*), a passage compared by scholars to related Sanskrit fragments and Vinaya accounts [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma]. In AN 5.123 and AN 5.124, the text enumerates the five qualities that make a sick person difficult to care for and the five factors that render an attendant unfit or fit to nurse the sick [Anālayo 2016]. Other discourses, such as the *Upajjhaṭṭhanasutta* (AN 5.57), set forth five subjects for daily contemplation [Walsh 2013].
Textual parallels and cross-corpus reuse are extensive. SuttaCentral records parallels for suttas of the *Pañcakanipāta* across Chinese Āgamas—chiefly the *Ekottarikāgama* (EĀ and EA2), *Saṁyuktāgama* (SĀ), and *Madhyamāgama* (MĀ)—as well as individual Chinese translations, Sanskrit collections such as the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT) [SuttaCentral]. Automatically computed text-reuse data from DharmaNexus identifies over 94,000 matching segments between AN 5 and 656 other Pali texts, showing the densest internal overlap with adjacent nipātas of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (AN 4, AN 10, AN 3, AN 8, and AN 6), the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (SN 46, SN 35, SN 37), Vinaya Khandhakas (Kd 1, Kd 17), and the *Puggalapaññatti* (Pp 2.5) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns AN 5 discourses with the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (T 99), *Ekottarikāgama* (T 125), and *Madhyamāgama* (T 26), Sanskrit witnesses including the *Arthaviniścayasūtra* and *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, and Tibetan translations such as the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (D 6) and Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D 4094) [DharmaNexus].
